note: The routing table as DATA, not code. A table compiled into the guards goes stale the moment a lineup changes, and it goes stale silently — the guards keep running and simply stop classifying correctly. CORRECTED 2026-09-23 (effort-versions.md research): a Claude Code subagent DEFINITION with no `effort` frontmatter does NOT fall back to this model default; per code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents it INHERITS the orchestrating session's current effort. Every effort-taking model has this hazard, not just opus — state effort explicitly rather than relying on inheritance; spawn-guard.mjs warns and the agent-defs audit check flags any definition with a model but no effort, opus included.

OFFICIAL (whats-new-fable-5-1): same $10/$50 as Fable 5; cache reads at a quarter of the cost ($0.25/MTok, re-verified live 2026-09-23). A long session with a stable prefix is cheaper than sticker price implies - verify the number before relying on it. 2026-10-06: Fable's plan weight is UNVERIFIED (the measured data fits about 3x Sonnet, not the 5x its API price ratio suggests); planUsageMultipliers deliberately has no fable entry.

COMMUNITY, first-hand (Every.to, TheNeuronDaily): "sticks to what you tell it" is CONTESTED. Reports of overshooting explicit limits (1,000 words -> 1,288; 8-12 quotes -> 43, 5 fabricated) and unprompted style decisions. The friction is over-inference, not literalism. Do not route on an adherence claim.

COMMUNITY, first-hand (dev.to): the gap over Opus/Sonnet is procedural discipline, not intelligence - stating a hypothesis before editing, labelling claims VERIFIED/REASONED/ASSUMED. A brief that carries that checklist closes most of the gap on a cheaper tier, which is exactly what the warrant is meant to make you ask.

referenceModelsNote: Non-routable reference entries for OLDER pinned model ids, so an agent definition pinned to a full/dated id (not an alias) is classified as premium/non-premium correctly by classifyModel() (unchanged — these ids already match the current alias tier's regex loosely) AND has its EFFORT validated against what that specific model actually supports via classifyReferenceModel()/referenceEffortSupported() in hooks/lib/context.mjs, rather than against the current alias tier's (possibly wider) effort list. Source: live-docs.md §1, fetched 2026-09-23. Not part of `routing` — nothing routes here, they exist only for validation of an id someone already pinned.
availabilityNote: An entry with available:false is still classified, but an agent definition pinned to it is a finding. A model you cannot reach fails at spawn time with nothing having warned you beforehand, and the failure surfaces as a broken agent rather than as a configuration mistake. Set available:false for anything outside your plan.
unknownNote: A model matching no entry is treated as PREMIUM and flagged. Defaulting an unrecognised model to cheap would let a new top-tier model bypass the warrant and the cap on the day it ships — the exact window in which nobody has updated the table yet. Fail toward the expensive assumption; the cost of a spurious warrant is one line in a brief.

low.note: skip thinking; reads and single commands

xhigh.note: recommended start for agentic work on current top tiers

max.note: reserve for genuinely frontier problems; large cost for small gain

effortNote: Ranks are global so two agents on different models stay comparable — the reviewer-parity rule needs that. The supported SET is per-tier, under each entry's "efforts", because availability genuinely differs by model. An effort not in a tier's list is not a smaller amount of thinking; it is a parameter that model does not take.

3.label: moderate — bounded multi-step, parse structured output

routingNote: Task weight 1-5 maps to a model AND an effort. Round DOWN when uncertain and escalate on failure; over-provisioning is a rule violation, not a safety margin. Weight 4 may take opus where blast radius warrants it. Nothing routes to fable — it is an exception, not a row.

ladderToolsNote: Each ladder worker's frontmatter `disallowedTools` is GENERATED from this block by scripts/routing-table.mjs --sync-agent-descriptions (--check-agent-descriptions fails on drift). `everywhere` is dropped from every ladder agent: Artifact (an exact tool name, so ArtifactComments, ArtifactData and ArtifactCheck are listed beside it) and the desktop-only servers (visualize, terminal, ccd_session) cost about 15K tokens at the start of every spawn and ran in 7 of 1,175 ladder runs in 30 days (Artifact 7, ccd_session 17 via mark_chapter/spawn_task, terminal 1, visualize 0); the other ccd_* servers and mcp-registry had 0-1 uses. `browserOnly` (the Claude_Browser, claude-in-chrome and computer-use servers, about 8K tokens with their instructions) is dropped from every agent except a ladderVariants entry with `browser: true`: 39 runs (3.3%) drove the browser, 19 of them on sonnet/high, 4 used claude-in-chrome, none computer-use. `keepOn` names a server dropped everywhere except the listed agents: ccd_session_mgmt (session lookups and polling) stays on ac-haiku, 2 of its 44 runs. Server-level entries (mcp__<server>) are the only MCP form the docs list for disallowedTools besides mcp__<server>__* and mcp__*; no glob such as mcp__ccd_* is used. Account-specific connectors carry per-account ids (a Claude Docs connector, a Gmail connector) and are NOT listed. Kept on purpose, because the numbers do not pay: scheduled-tasks (11 runs, about 65 tokens of names) and the agent-bus and cloudflare servers (24 and 30 runs). general-purpose and the lead keep every tool.

ladderVariants.role: UI and browser work: drive a page or dev server, screenshot, read the console
UI and browser work that needs opus capability

ladderVariantsNote: A variant is NOT a rung: it has no number and is never an escalation target, and routing never picks it (rungFor() reads `ladder` only). It is one rung's model and effort (`base`) plus a different tool set, spawnable by name like a rung and counted as a ladder agent by every guard (isLadderAgentName). The rungs drop the browser servers, so UI work goes to ac-browser (sonnet/high, where half the observed browser runs landed) or ac-browser-opus (opus/medium, Opus 5.5's own default effort); recommend.mjs --browser names them. A heavier UI task: split it (the logic on a rung, the browser check on a variant) or drive the browser from the lead.
ladderCacheTtlNote: A ladder rung's own optional `cacheTtl` field ("1h", or omitted for the 5m subagent default) is GENERATED into that rung's agents/<agent>.md frontmatter as a nested `experimental: { cacheTtl: "1h" }` block by scripts/routing-table.mjs --sync-agent-descriptions (same generator, same --check/--sync pair as the description text) — never hand-edit the block in the file. NO rung carries it today: it was set on rungs 7-10 (ac-opus-medium/high/xhigh/max) in release 0.29.17 (2026-09-26) and removed again in 0.29.30 (2026-10-03, operator choice). From 2026-10-02T16Z to 2026-10-03, 1h cache writes cost 242 plan units (23% of the total); agents run continuously and compact often, so the 1h TTL never paid off (it only pays when an agent sits idle for more than 5 minutes) and each rewrite costs 1.6x a 5m write. The field and its generator stay so a rung can be put back on 1h with a one-line config edit plus --sync-agent-descriptions.
ladderRoleNote: Each rung's `role` is the capability shape its agents/<agent>.md description opens with. It must never say how OFTEN a rung is used or which task types route to it: scripts/routing-table.mjs --sync-agent-descriptions appends that from the live routes, and --check-agent-descriptions fails when a description, a rung or a file drifts from this list. The one routing claim a role may make is 'default for <type>', which the check verifies against the live routes; any other routing word in a role (default, rare, prefer, usually, often, typically, reserve, weight-N) fails the check.
ladderNote: The routing grid (weight x kind, floored by consequence) still picks (model, effort) exactly as before — this ladder does not change that logic, it is the ORDERED VIEW of the same (model, effort) pairs, cheapest to dearest, each mapped to a spawnable generic worker definition under agents/ (namespaced <plugin>:<agent> when spawned from outside this repo, e.g. agent-companion:ac-sonnet-medium) because the Agent tool has no per-spawn effort parameter — effort is locked to whichever definition's frontmatter is used. Fable is deliberately NOT a rung: it sits outside the ladder as a warranted exception (see the fable tier's warrantCriterion), never a routine destination. The CURRENT weight defaults (1-2 haiku, 3 sonnet/medium=rung 3, 4 sonnet/high=rung 4, 5 opus/xhigh=rung 9) are UNCHANGED by adding this view — see `routing` and `taskKinds` for what actually picks a rung; a pending research finding may revise those defaults later as a pure data edit, without touching the ladder shape itself. Consequence floors already raise the rung the same way they raise effort/model in effortFor(): `elevated` floors effort at `high` (>= rung 4 within whichever model the weight already picked), `critical` floors the model at opus AND the effort at xhigh (>= rung 9).

mechanical.note: Small answer space with one right shape. More thinking does not produce a better result, it produces the same result more slowly.

examples: a feature against a clear spec
bounded.note: The shape is known; the work is filling it in correctly.

diagnostic.note: A search problem. The answer exists but must be found, and more passes genuinely raise the odds of finding it.

novel-design.note: Large answer space with no known-good shape to copy. Each additional pass tends to surface a failure mode that would otherwise ship.

taskKindNote: Weight sets the MODEL — how much capability the task needs. Kind adjusts the EFFORT — how much the answer benefits from search. They are orthogonal: a routing table and a message bus can touch the same number of files and deserve completely different amounts of thinking. Compute effort as routing[weight].effort shifted by taskKinds[kind].effortDelta, clamped to the efforts table. When the kind is unclear, use bounded and escalate on failure rather than pre-paying for search you may not need.

reviewerParity.liveEvidence: operator-local live study, 2026-09-27: 789 real subagent spawns, 2026-09-21 to 09-27: code reviews at xhigh were clean 26/26 vs 18/21 at high (suggestive, p≈0.08), and live xhigh reviews cost in line with pre-trial xhigh reviews (about 1.25x, thin sample) -- what grew under the 2026-09-27 routes was the NUMBER of reviews, not the cost per review. recommend.mjs and evaluate.mjs size a reviewer to the writer (--writer): a writer raised to xhigh (large-refactor, novel-design) gets a reviewer at xhigh or above, so xhigh reviews are not reserved for critical changes. At spawn time a review brief's WRITER line (WRITER: opus/xhigh, or an agent name) lets spawn-guard size the reviewer the same way, judged in notes only, never a deny; with no WRITER line it checks only the critical-change floor (F1).
reviewerParity.note: A reviewer is sized to the writer it gates, never below it. Its MODEL is at least the writer's: a weaker reviewer catches the errors it would itself have avoided and waves through the ones it would itself have made, which is the novel-error class a stronger writer produces. Its EFFORT may go higher and must not go lower — refutation is a search problem and can need more thinking than generation did. The floors then apply as on any route: F1 raises a critical review to at least the critical floor (opus/xhigh) whatever the writer; F2 caps a fable writer's reviewer to the best tier that is a routing destination (opus, which still demands a WARRANT); F4 refuses a writer the table cannot size (a model outside the tier table, one unavailable with no staged replacement, or an effort that is no effort level) and fits the effort to what the reviewer's model accepts (none on haiku). modelMustMatch means the reviewer starts at the writer's model.

elevated.note: A mistake here costs other people time but is recoverable.

critical.note: A mistake here is expensive or irreversible.

consequenceNote: Consequence is a FLOOR, not a delta, and it is applied AFTER the kind adjustment so it cannot be undercut. This matters because difficulty and consequence are close to orthogonal: a one-line production migration is mechanical by KIND, which would otherwise push its effort DOWN on precisely the change most likely to hurt. The floor is the answer to "how bad is it if this is wrong", which is a different question from "how hard is this to get right".
architectureClassNote: `architectureClass: true` on a task type (integration, large-refactor, novel-design, critical-change ship with it; a local profile type may carry it too) marks it as never allowed to resolve to opus/low, at ANY layer, whatever its consequence happens to be (F6 in hooks/lib/context.mjs's resolveRoute()). Added 2026-09-24 as a backstop against a future config mistake -- e.g. a new consequence naming a model floor with no matching effort floor, or a trial/profile row's F5 waiver (see integration's override below) being misread as license to go all the way to low. Unlike F5, F6 is never waivable: a routing-profile row naming opus/low for an architecture-class type is refused at validation, in both read and write mode, not silently raised.

operate.summary: execute an ordered procedure or change a live system — even when every individual step looks trivial in isolation

selfReview.rationale: Operator decision 2026-10-06 (DECISIONS.md, "lean worker shape; main session stays unblocked"): every change gets ONE separate reviewer at the writer's tier, spawned by the writer, never only for risky changes (the operator rejected that gate). A writer of any listed type (the stand-alone writer types; mechanical-edit and subagent-worker are the edit workers a writer spawns for a 15+ call job and are covered by that writer's own review, so listing them would give a change two reviews; read-only types and parity types stay out), whose brief has no `REVIEW: lead` line, commits, spawns ONE parity reviewer in the foreground on its own rung (TYPE: code-review, WRITER: its own model/effort, the lead's brief verbatim, the diff range, the review file path), runs `fixRounds` (one) fix round on blocker and should-fix findings, never re-reviews, LANDS its own work (merge, plus verify the deploy where the repo deploys on merge, and every release gate the repo's CLAUDE.md requires stays), and returns the reviewer's verdict line verbatim, the review path, the post-fix sha and any disputed findings. The lead settles disputed findings and spot-checks the review file. Why: every lead-routed review costs two lead round-trips (spawn reviewer, then resume or re-spawn the writer), each stalling on the lead being free, and the fix round often starts on a cold cache; done by the writer, the fix round runs on its warm cache. Risk: the writer frames its own review; mitigated by the fixed brief the protocol dictates (the lead's brief verbatim, no scoping of the reviewer), the verbatim verdict line, and the lead spot-checking the review file. Cost history: a reviewer costs about 9.85 plan units per spawn on xhigh against 3.78 on opus/medium (2026-10-02 usage review: 172 units in the week when only xhigh writers carried it); 2026-10-02 had narrowed the list to novel-design and critical-change, and 2026-10-06 reverses that narrowing. The protocol text is GENERATED into the body of every agents/ac-*.md rung that is currently the default route for one of these types (scripts/routing-table.mjs --sync-agent-descriptions; --check-agent-descriptions fails on drift), so a routing-table move carries it along; a listed type spawned on any other ladder rung (a routing profile or local override can put it there) gets the same text, sized to that rung, appended to its brief at spawn. hooks/spawn-guard.mjs denies a code-review spawned by an agent that was itself spawned as a code-review (reviewers never spawn reviewers; positive match only). Reverse: empty `types`, or put `REVIEW: lead` in briefs.

taskTypesNote: A task type is a named preset over (weight, kind, consequence). Resolve it through the same grid as everything else; do not special-case it. "parity" as a weight means: sized to the writer being reviewed (at least its model and effort, then the floors; see reviewerParity). "inherit" as a consequence means: take the consequence of the change under review. Provenance is recorded per entry because these WILL go stale - the scout re-checks the lineup, and a routing review should re-read the sources, not the table. `--type` is now the PREFERRED input over `--weight`/`--kind` alone, because a named type is the only place the measured evidence (`override`, below) attaches — resolving by raw weight/kind bypasses it and falls back to the grid. An entry may carry an `override` block ({model, effort, reason, evidence, trialSince, reviewBy}, plus `overridesKindDelta: true` where it deliberately bypasses the kind's effort delta) recording a ROUTING TRIAL: a benchmark-backed (model, effort) pair that supersedes this entry's own weight/kind/consequence grid resolution for the stated trial window. It applies only when the type is resolved as-is (no explicit --weight/--kind/--consequence that departs from the preset); passing an explicit weight/kind/consequence that DEPARTS from the preset answers a different question and falls back to the plain grid, while one EQUAL to the preset restates the type and keeps the override. The weight/kind/consequence fields on an overridden entry are kept unchanged for provenance and for `--list`/weight-only callers — only the resolved (model, effort) changes. A type with no `override` is UNBENCHMARKED by this trial and keeps its grid-resolved routing unchanged; say so explicitly rather than leaving it ambiguous.

cacheTtl.note: Per-definition prompt-cache TTL recommendation. Not enforced by any guard — set it yourself in a subagent's own frontmatter as a NESTED key, `experimental: { cacheTtl: "1h" }` (i.e. `cacheTtl` lives under `experimental`, not at the top level of the frontmatter). Requires Claude Code v2.1.248+; Claude Code ignores `1h` there while the subscription is drawing on usage credits (falls back to 5m). Default stays 5m for every definition unless called out below.

recommendOneHourFor.criterion: opus-tier definitions (model resolves to the `opus` alias or an opus reference id) whose name or description marks them long-lived / resumed — architect, reviewer, lead roles
recommendOneHourFor.why: These are the roles the evidence shows actually get resumed more than 5 minutes after their last turn, or sit through long tool waits (test suites, builds, CI). 1h converts what would be a full ~250-340K-token rewrite into a cheap cache read.

cacheTtl.ladderWorkersExcludedNote: The generic ac-* ladder workers (ac-haiku, ac-sonnet-*, ac-opus-*) stay on the 5m subagent default, even at opus tiers (ac-opus-low/medium/high/xhigh/max). 1h writes bill at 2x the base input price against 1.25x for 5m, and these workers run continuously and compact often, so the cache is rewritten long before an hour passes and the 1h TTL has nothing to earn back; it pays only for an agent that sits idle more than 5 minutes. ac-opus-medium/high/xhigh/max were briefly on 1h (0.29.17 to 0.29.29, 2026-09-26 to 2026-10-03); that was reverted 2026-10-03 after 1h writes cost 242 plan units (23% of the total) from 2026-10-02T16Z. The 1h recommendation above is for the long-lived, resumed roles (architect/reviewer/lead definitions), not these workers.

evidence.method: 30-day measurement (2026-08-24 to 2026-09-23), 1,407 subagent transcripts with billable requests, 100% of in-window subagent transcripts, 84,843 subagent requests reconstructed from usage fields.
evidence.figures: Cache-hit ratio 99.8% under a 5-minute gap, 13.3% in the 5-60 minute gap, 4.4% beyond 60 minutes — the 5-minute cliff is real. Switching every subagent to 1h is roughly cost-neutral overall (-0.46% of subagent cost, -$32/30d). By model tier: Opus 5.5 -12.0%, Opus 5 -4.7%, Opus 4.8 +4.1%, Sonnet 5 +2.9%, Haiku 4.5 +15.9%. Opus-tier-only 1h (this recommendation's scope): -2.1% of subagent cost (-$144/30d). Break-even: 1h wins for a tier once 5-60m rewrites exceed roughly 39.5% of that tier's cache-write tokens (~1.0-1.1% of requests); observed 35.7% overall, but Opus 5 alone was already at 51.5% (above break-even) while Sonnet sat at 29.3% (below it). By agent type, the pattern is architects/reviewers save under 1h (project-specific architect roles measured -12.9% and -6.1%, project-specific reviewer roles -4.2% to -4.9%) while one-shot builders/general-purpose workers cost more (a project-specific sonnet builder role +8.2%, general-purpose@opus +6.9%).

cacheTtl.remeasureNote: Re-run the report's scripts (~/.claude/reports/2026-09-23-subagent-cache-ttl-scripts/) after two weeks of the resume-window doctrine change (the doctrine patch is kept outside this repo). Turn on the global 1h setting (`subagentPromptCacheTtl`) if subagent rewrites in the 5-60m band exceed ~40% of write tokens overall, or if Sonnet alone crosses the ~39.5% break-even.

docsVerifiedLive.frontmatterField: `experimental.cacheTtl` — a nested map key under the subagent frontmatter's `experimental` field, values `5m` or `1h` only (anything else ignored). Requires Claude Code v2.1.248+. Ignored for `1h` while the subscription is on usage credits.
precedence: a subagent definition's own experimental.cacheTtl frontmatter — THIS recommendation lives here, and is overridden by any of the three controls above
the bucket default: 5m for subagents/workflows/forks/compaction/titles regardless of subscription, vs 1h for the main conversation on a subscription within plan usage
docsVerifiedLive.oneHourWriteMultiplier: 1h cache writes bill at 2x the base input-token price, vs 1.25x for 5m writes; cache reads are 0.1x base input either way. No long-context surcharge.

planUsageMultipliers.note: Relative PLAN-USAGE burn per unit of (price-weighted) token cost -- NOT api dollar pricing. Plan usage windows deplete at a rate the sticker price does not predict, per the operator's own in-app observation. Keyed by tier alias (see tiers, above); a tier with no entry here gets no plan-usage index computed by bench/runner.mjs's rebuildSummary() rather than a guessed number -- fail toward 'unknown', not toward inventing a multiplier nobody measured.

sonnet.source: baseline (defined as 1.0); every other multiplier here is relative to it

opus.source: in-app tooltip, 2026-09-23, undocumented; 2026-10-06: fits the limit recalibration at about 1.45-1.5x, and nothing shows it is introductory (the 09-23 guess is the operator's, recorded here as history)

planUsageMultipliersNote: Measured 2026-09-23: Opus 5.5 = 1.5x Sonnet 5 per an in-app plan-usage tooltip reading (API pricing is 2x -- the plan-usage rate and the dollar rate are NOT the same number, which is the whole reason this table exists separately from `tiers.*.resolvesTo.pricing`). 2026-10-06 note: this is a per-TOKEN plan weight (about 1.45-1.5x; it fits the size of the weekly limit, and there is no evidence it is introductory, though the operator guessed so on 09-23); per CALL at equal context Opus 5.5 costs about 1.9x Sonnet, because it writes more output. No haiku or fable reading exists yet -- do not extrapolate one. Reads note (cache-read-weight-2026-09-23, same date): this multiplier is an aggregate index over a whole cell's token mix, not a read-specific weight -- the Opus-vs-Sonnet ratio for cache READS ALONE is separately UNMEASURED (see costDrivers.planUsageWeighting below); don't treat the 1.5x figure as answering the read question too.

costDrivers.note: Across this machine's real sessions, CACHE READS are the largest cost bucket -- not output tokens. Reads = context size x number of requests, so TURN COUNT and CONTEXT SIZE drive cost more than output tokens do. The two levers: fewer turns per task (less back-and-forth, more done per tool-call batch), and a smaller stable context (less to re-read on every turn). Cache TTL (`cacheTtl` above) only decides re-read vs re-write pricing AFTER an idle gap -- it does not change how many reads happen or how large each one is, so raising TTL is not a substitute for cutting turns or context.

readPricePerMTokByTier.note: Cache-hit ($/MTok) rate per tier, read from tiers.*.resolvesTo.pricing.cacheHitPerMTok above -- kept here too as a flat lookup for a reader who wants the number without walking the tier objects. Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5 read at the SAME $0.20/MTok, so the per-read price is equal. It does NOT make Opus cost the same as Sonnet: measured 2026-10-06, per call at equal context Opus 5.5 is about 1.9x Sonnet (it writes more output), and its plan weight is about 1.5x per token.

planUsageWeighting.note: How cache reads weigh against the Max plan's usage window is not published anywhere Anthropic states it, unlike the API dollar rate above. Plan metering of cache READS is roughly API-price-proportional: 40.1M Sonnet 5 cache reads moved the 5-hour usage meter ~2 points (~0.05 pts per 1M reads, range 0.025-0.075). ~3.95M cache WRITES moved it ~4 points, so per token, writes cost roughly 20x what reads do -- the same direction and order of magnitude as the API list-price ratio (~12.5x). Conclusion: cache MISSES (re-writes) are the expensive event on this plan, not reads. The Opus 5.5 vs Sonnet 5 per-read plan-usage ratio is UNMEASURED -- the Opus arm of this experiment hit a harness caching anomaly (separate claude -p processes do not reliably share prompt cache even with byte-identical content, including --resume; see docs/BENCHMARK.md "Caching") before a clean reading could be taken. Do not extrapolate an Opus read weight from the Sonnet figure.
planUsageWeighting.dataPath: benchmarks/cache-read-weight-2026-09-23/ under this machine's agent-companion data dir (dataDir())

reviewer-effort-direction.question: Does a reviewer at HIGHER effort than the writer catch more, or less?
reviewer-effort-direction.tension: Our rule says effort may exceed and must not drop. One first-hand report (Wavect) found high-effort review slower and lower-recall than low. Willison observed that past high, Fable drafts the deliverable in thinking and rewrites it - double cost, no gain. Against that, the operator-local live study, 2026-09-27: 789 real subagent spawns, 2026-09-21 to 09-27 found code reviews at xhigh clean 26/26 vs 18/21 at high (suggestive, p≈0.08), at a cost per review in line with pre-trial xhigh reviews (about 1.25x, thin sample).
reviewer-effort-direction.measure: From telemetry: for reviews, compare findings-per-review and post-merge defect rate by reviewer effort relative to writer effort. Needs reviewers to report findings structurally.

fable-cache-economics.question: Does Fable 5.1 cache-read pricing make long stable-prefix sessions competitive with Opus?
fable-cache-economics.tension: Official: cache reads at a quarter of the cost ($0.25/MTok). Our measured cache hit ratio is ~96%. Fable is now 2.5x Opus on sticker price (was 2x, before Opus 5.5 dropped to $4/$20) - the cache discount has a wider gap to close than it did. At max effort output tokens run ~1.7x Fable 5 - the discount may be eaten by verbosity. 2026-10-06: Fable's plan weight is unverified (the data fits about 3x Sonnet, not 5x), so no plan-unit saving or cost from this discount is established.
fable-cache-economics.measure: From telemetry: per-session cost by model with cache-read share. Compare fable vs opus on sessions of similar turn count.

sonnet-vs-opus-at-weight-5.question: Is Sonnet 5 sufficient for some weight-5 work?
sonnet-vs-opus-at-weight-5.tension: Vendor benchmarks put Sonnet 5 above Opus 5 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and some agentic evals at ~40% less cost. Vendor-run, and an outlier.
sonnet-vs-opus-at-weight-5.measure: From telemetry: escalation rate (a Sonnet spawn re-run at Opus) by task type. If weight-5 bounded work rarely escalates from Sonnet, lower the base.

procedural-checklist-vs-tier.question: Does a verification checklist in the brief substitute for a higher tier?
procedural-checklist-vs-tier.tension: First-hand: teaching Opus/Sonnet the Fable-style checklist (hypothesis before edit, VERIFIED/REASONED/ASSUMED labels) closes most of the gap. If true, many Fable warrants should be declined in favour of a better brief.
procedural-checklist-vs-tier.measure: From telemetry: warrant acceptance rate, and outcome of warranted Fable spawns vs Opus spawns with a checklist brief on the same task type.
